article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Math-gender Misconceptions Questionnaire short version (MGMQ-s)
description: The MGMQ-s is the pre- and post-test measure of teachers' math-gender misconceptions. It "consists of two misconceptions scales (empathizing-systemizing ... and girls' compensation" with four items each, plus eight correct filler items to balance the questionnaire. For each item participants indicate agreement dichotomously and certainty on a five-point Likert scale; misconception scores are computed by multiplying agreement (−1/+1) by certainty (0–4), yielding item values from −4 to +4, with higher scores expressing stronger misconceptions. Items are presented in a newly randomized order per participant.
requirements: A criterion determines a misconception as prevalent if a participant agreed to at least one item per scale with high certainty (certain or absolutely certain)
target_learning_goals: measuring empathizing-systemizing and girls' compensation misconceptions
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test in the 2×2 experiment; conceptual change scores were calculated by subtracting pre-test from post-test results
key_sources: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9

article_title: The impact of active mentorship: results from a survey of faculty in the Department of Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.
citation: Walensky Rochelle P., Kim Younji, Chang Yuchiao, Porneala Bianca C., Bristol Mirar N., Armstrong Katrina, Campbell Eric G. (2018). The impact of active mentorship: results from a survey of faculty in the Department of Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1191-5
title: MGH faculty mentorship survey with a 10-area mentorship quality score
description: A 12-page, ~15-minute electronic survey administered via REDCap to 988 full-time Department of Medicine faculty, yielding 553 responses (56.0%). Mentorship was defined as "someone who serves as a career role model and who advises, guides and promotes his or her mentee's career or training." Mentorship quality was rated on a 5-point Likert scale across ten areas, averaged and dichotomized as low (< 3) or high (≥ 3) for respondents answering at least 5 of 10 questions. Outcomes included having a mentor, mentoring role, stalled in rank, and job satisfaction.
requirements: Respondents must answer at least 5 of the 10 mentorship quality questions to receive a score
constraints: Mentorship quality was assessed only among faculty who currently had a mentor
The stalled-in-rank variable excludes faculty with the rank of Professor
examples: Survey disseminated June 1, 2016 with reminders on June 8, 15, and 27; closed June 30, 2016; 21.3% of those with a current mentor gave a low quality score
key_sources: Walensky Rochelle P., Kim Younji, Chang Yuchiao, Porneala Bianca C., Bristol Mirar N., Armstrong Katrina, Campbell Eric G. (2018). The impact of active mentorship: results from a survey of faculty in the Department of Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1191-5
